note: The £13,500 deposit matches to the pound the £13,500 cash withdrawn on 13 June for a private car purchase, which the June review verified with the advert. The customer told us the same day that the sale fell through.
lesson: A cash deposit that exactly matches an earlier cash withdrawal, whose purpose was already verified, is the customer's own money coming back and can be closed if the explanation fits the earlier review. Send an RFI if the amounts differ or the original purpose was never verified. Escalate if the customer has withdrawn and redeposited cash like this before.

note: The £11,850 cash deposit matches to the pound the signed sale receipt for the customer's 2019 saloon (GA19 XNQ), dated the day before. The insurance schedule shows the customer insured that same car, so they owned it to sell.
lesson: A large cash deposit is explained when there's a sale receipt signed by both parties for the same amount, dated shortly before the deposit, and a separate document showing the customer owned the item. Send an RFI if the amount, date or item details don't match, or if there's no proof of ownership. Escalate if the customer keeps making large cash "sales" or the documents contradict each other.

note: The £46,887.20 arrived by faster payment from Wendale Solicitors LLP's client account, referenced "Estate of Avery Lockmere". It matches to the penny the solicitor's letter of 14 September confirming the inheritance and saying payment would be made that week. Without it, inflows are just the school salary, within profile. (Labelled THIRD_PARTY_DOCUMENTED; changed to DOCUMENTED_EVENT because the README lists inheritance under it.)
lesson: A large one-off credit is explained when it comes directly from a regulated firm's client account, its reference matches a letter from that firm, and the amount and timing match the letter. The payment itself confirms the customer is the beneficiary, even if the letter doesn't name them. Send an RFI if the money comes from anyone other than the firm named in the letter, or if the amount or reference doesn't match. Escalate if the letter looks unreliable or the money leaves the account quickly to third parties.

note: The four deposits (£37,470) are the weekly takings from the two car parks. Each one matches to the pound a numbered safe bag on the collection reports. Each was paid in the morning after its site was emptied: Everwell on Sundays, Cranton on Mondays, exactly as the 2024 cash procedure says. About £19k a week is plausible for £1.7m turnover, and the May 2026 review closed the same pattern. Repeated cash deposits just under a threshold are not structuring when each one is a separate site's routine takings. Close only if a cash procedure written before the alert sets the schedule, collection records match each deposit's amount and date, and the volume fits declared turnover. Escalate if deposits don't match the collection records, cash from different sites or days is combined or split, the timing breaks the schedule, or amounts keep clustering just under the threshold more tightly than normal takings would.

The ten £245 payments are friends paying their share of a group trip to Lisbon. The booking, dated 3 October (before any money arrived), lists 11 travellers at £245 each, £2,695 in total, due by 15 October, with the customer as lead traveller. The payers shown are named on it and their references say "Lisbon" or "Trip". The money out within 48 hours is the booking being paid on time, topped up from the customer's own salary.
lesson: Many small, equal payments from different people that are quickly paid out are not money mule activity when the customer is collecting for a group purchase they lead. Close if a booking or invoice dated before the money came in names the payers, the per-person amount matches each payment, and the money goes out to the merchant on the booking by the due date. Send an RFI if payers aren't named on the booking, the amounts differ from the per-person price, or the outgoing payee isn't the merchant. Escalate if money goes to unrelated third parties or the pattern repeats with no new booking.

note: Four cash deposits of just under £10k each (£37,905 in total) at two locations. The reconciliation REC-975 is dated 16 October but records the bar and food court takings as "banked 17 Oct", a day after it was written. All the evidence is the company's own summary. There's no till or ticketing data, no price list (the gate averages £23.16 and £22.77 per ticket differ), and no earlier review showing this is how they normally bank. We need the festival's own records for 14-15 October to confirm the takings.
lesson: Several cash deposits just under a threshold, each linked to a separate revenue stream, can only be closed when the business's summary is backed by records produced independently of it (till Z-reports, ticketing system data, price lists) or by a banking practice that has already been reviewed. Check that each document is dated on or after the events it records; a document reporting a deposit that hadn't happened yet is a reliability flag. Send an RFI for business records if the only evidence is the customer's own summary or there's a date or arithmetic inconsistency. Escalate if the independent records don't match, or the amounts keep landing just under the threshold across events.

note: The £18,100 came from Sandley Finance Ltd and matches the principal on the car loan agreement signed on 10 August. The £19,350 paid out the next day went to Kingsbrook Motors Ltd with reference "INV 16177" and matches the dealer invoice to the customer for a used hatchback; the customer topped it up by £1,250 from their own salary. The loan was spent on what it was for. Minor residual notes: the invoice says "2020" but the registration is a 21 plate, and the invoice is dated the day before the payment.
lesson: Money that arrives and leaves quickly is not a pass-through concern when a loan is paid out for a stated purpose and spent on it. Close if a loan agreement shows the same lender, amount and purpose as the credit, and the outgoing payment goes to a merchant whose invoice matches the amount, customer and purpose. Small differences on third-party documents (model year vs registration, invoice dated on the sale day) are residual notes when the money trail matches. Send an RFI for purpose documents if the payee or amount doesn't match the invoice. Escalate if loan money goes to individuals or unrelated parties, or several loans are taken out in quick succession.

note: The list entry BK-L57749 is Sidney Wenton, who ran Talworth Imports Ltd from Unit 4B. The payee is Lockwick Print Studio Ltd, registered at Unit 4A and owned by Noel Norcombe (born 1996). The only overlap is the building, Faldale Works: different unit, different company, different person. The £210 matches the course confirmation and the payment reference, and fits a civil engineer's everyday spending. A watch-list hit on a shared address is a false match when the payee's own records show a different unit, company name, director and owner from the listed subject, and the payment's purpose and size fit the customer's profile. Compare names, dates of birth, company names and the exact unit before deciding; a shared building or business park isn't a link. Escalate if the payee shares any person, company, director, owner or exact unit with the listed subject, or if the payments are large, repeated or out of character for the customer.

The single £10,026.94 SWIFT payment went straight to Alddale University Medical Center in Beirut. It matches to the penny the hospital's invoice of 18 October for Charlie Sandton's coronary bypass surgery, and the payment reference names the patient. The customer explained it unprompted when asked (paying for their parent's heart surgery), and the shared surname fits. The money went to an institution, not an individual. It's a one-off with no other Lebanon activity, and nothing else on the account was flagged.
lesson: A single payment to a higher-risk country is explained when it goes directly to an identifiable institution (hospital, university, government body) and matches an invoice from that institution in payee, amount and purpose, and the customer's explanation fits the invoice. Check the payee is the institution itself, not an individual or a third-party account. Send an RFI for purpose documents if there's no invoice, the payee differs from the invoicing body, or the amount doesn't match. Send an RFI for source of funds if the payment clearly exceeds what the customer could have saved. Escalate if payments to the country repeat or grow, go to individuals, or the payee raises a sanctions concern.

note: The £23,754.79 came from Talfield Life Assurance plc with reference "CLAIM 76654". It matches to the penny the insurer's letter of 10 September accepting the customer's critical illness claim and saying it would be paid directly to them. A critical illness payout also plausibly explains why the account went quiet: the customer was likely off work, with no salary since January. The mobile number change in July passed security checks and on its own isn't a concern. (Labelled THIRD_PARTY_DOCUMENTED; changed to DOCUMENTED_EVENT because the README lists payouts under it.)
lesson: A dormant account that comes back to life with one large credit is explained when the payer is a regulated firm (insurer, pension provider, solicitor), the reference and amount match that firm's letter addressed to the customer, and the money is paid directly to the customer. Check the dormant period for account-takeover signs: contact details changed, new devices or payees, and quick outflows after the credit. Close if the credit is documented and nothing has changed suspiciously. Send an RFI for an updated profile if the customer's circumstances have clearly changed (e.g. salary stopped). Escalate if contact details changed and the funds then leave quickly to new or third-party payees.

note: The £1,100 faster payment to "Kai Langwell" matched list entry BK-L91462 on name only. The listed subject's relationship was ended in 2024 over unexplained third-party payments. Nothing on file identifies the payee (no invoice, address, business name or date of birth), so we can't confirm or rule out a match. The "Garden landscaping" reference and amount are plausible, but they're the customer's own description.
lesson: A watch-list hit on name alone can't be closed as a different party unless something on file tells the two apart (date of birth, address, company details, an invoice). If nothing does, send an RFI for counterparty details asking for an invoice and the payee's business details. Close as a different party when the payee's identifying details clearly differ from the listed subject. Escalate if the details match the listed subject (same address, date of birth or account), or the customer makes repeated or growing payments to them. Unrelated contact notes (statement requests, charge queries) are neither evidence for nor against.

note: A warehouse operative earning £1,100 a month received £12,900 from nine different individuals in about a week (7-13 September), on top of their salary. The references don't add up: "deposit", "invoice 2231", "loan", "for the phone", "laptop". Within 48 hours, 92% (£11,911.34) was paid out. The amounts, payers and references don't fit the declared profile, and the speed of the outflows points to money passing through the account, not the customer's own activity. This is the classic money mule pattern.
lesson: Several unrelated people paying in over a few days, with mixed references (goods, loans, invoices, deposits) that don't fit the customer's occupation or income, followed by most of the money leaving within 48 hours, is a money mule pattern. Escalate. Don't send an RFI: asking the customer can tip off the people controlling the account, and an explanation (e.g. "selling items online") rarely accounts for both the inflows and the fast outflows. Close only when one documented purpose covers every payer and the outgoing payee (e.g. a group booking naming all payers, paid to the merchant). Unrelated income across many payers with no single documented purpose is never "within profile".

note: Nine people each paid exactly £320 (£2,880 in total) over 3-7 August, all with matching "Edinburgh" or "Trip" references, and £3,328.70 went out within 48 hours. That looks like a group trip the customer is collecting for. Unlike the Lisbon case, though, there's no booking on file to confirm the payers, the per-person price or who the money went to. The outgoing payee isn't shown. The lost card note is unrelated.
lesson: Equal payments from several people with one consistent reference, quickly paid out, point to a group collection, not mule activity. The single, consistent purpose is what tells it apart from mule activity, where references are mixed and amounts vary. But without a booking or invoice on file it isn't evidenced: send an RFI for purpose documents. Close once a booking or invoice dated before the money came in names the payers, matches the per-person amount and shows the outflow going to that merchant. Escalate if the booking doesn't match, the outflows go to individuals, or the references and amounts start to vary.

note: Over 10-12 October, three UK individuals sent the customer £19,387.66, each with the reference "transfer". Within 1-3 days, four identical SWIFT payments of £4,119.88 (£16,479.52 in total) went to four different individuals in Lebanon, none sharing the customer's surname, all referenced "family support". Lebanon is higher risk and not a declared country. The money sent abroad came from third parties, not the customer's £2,650 salary. The only explanation is a vague one-line chat. This looks like the customer is moving other people's money to a higher-risk jurisdiction, possibly as an informal money transfer service.

£21,150 came from Talmore Finance Ltd as a "LOAN ADVANCE", and the next day £22,900 went to Hartwick Motors Ltd with reference "INV 33786", topped up by £1,750 of the customer's own money. That looks like a car bought on finance, the same pattern as case 7, but here neither the loan agreement nor the dealer invoice is on file, so the purpose isn't proven. The pattern is low risk, so an RFI rather than escalation. The statement request and the earlier bonus review are unrelated.
lesson: Loan money that arrives and quickly goes to a merchant matching the loan's apparent purpose (finance company to car dealer) is low risk but not evidenced without documents. Send an RFI for purpose documents: the loan agreement and the merchant invoice. Close once the agreement matches the lender, amount and purpose and the invoice matches the payee, amount and customer. A plausible pattern alone isn't enough to close. Escalate if loan money goes to individuals or unrelated parties, or several loans come in close together.

note: £15,045 came in from Wilholt Ventures Ltd, but that company was dissolved on 31 October 2025, so it shouldn't be able to make payments. The payment reference says "CONSULTANCY", but the customer says it's "a loan from a friend to help with bills". The next day, 90% (£13,540.50) went by SWIFT to an individual in Turkey with the reference "FAMILY", which contradicts the "bills" story too. A care worker on £1,500 a month receiving and forwarding money this way, with three explanations that don't agree, is a mule pattern.
lesson: Escalate when the payment reference, the customer's explanation and where the money went don't agree with each other. A single contradiction is grounds to escalate. Check the payer's company status: payments from a dissolved company are a serious red flag, because the account is likely misused or controlled by someone else. Money labelled as a loan for bills that's then sent abroad to an individual is not the customer's own spending. Don't send an RFI once the customer has already given an explanation that the evidence contradicts; asking again risks tipping off. An earlier closed review for an unrelated reason doesn't lower the risk.

note: Twelve cash deposits of £9,000-£9,999 (£114,680 in total) went in at three locations in ten days. That's more than the business's whole declared annual turnover (£111,000), and about 1.8 times its yearly cash sales (£63,771 per the management accounts), from a business that trades at weekend markets but deposited on weekdays. On 15 October the director asked staff whether keeping each deposit below £10,000 would avoid reporting and whether different branches are added together. After being told monitoring applies to any amount, they said they'd use a different branch. That is a stated intention to avoid reporting. The earlier December-peak review doesn't explain an October volume this size.
lesson: Escalate when cash deposits cluster just under a reporting threshold across several branches and the volume is far beyond what the business's own accounts support. Compare the deposits with the business's annual cash sales, not just its monthly turnover. A customer asking how to avoid reporting, or saying they'll switch branches after being told about monitoring, is direct evidence of structuring and on its own is grounds to escalate, whatever documents are on file. Don't send an RFI: the customer already knows they're being watched, and contacting them again risks tipping off. A previous closed review for seasonal peaks only covers that season and volume.

note: £56,700.77 arrived from Corwick Solicitors LLP's client account with reference "ESTATE OF KIT STANFIELD". That looks like an inheritance, the same pattern as case 3, but unlike case 3 there's no solicitor's letter or estate statement on file to confirm the customer is a beneficiary or the amount they're entitled to. Coming from a regulated firm's client account makes it low risk, but at about 16 months' salary it isn't evidenced yet. The statement request is unrelated.

The £8,662.41 SWIFT credit from Calcote Hotel and Gardens in Lebanon is a refund of the wedding venue deposit the customer paid to the same venue in June. That deposit was reviewed and closed on 26 June with the booking contract on file. The venue's email of 5 September confirms the cancellation and a full refund of £8,662.41 for BOOKING 31135, which matches the payment amount and reference. Money coming back from the same counterparty it was sent to, via the same corridor, adds no new risk.
lesson: A credit from a higher-risk country is explained when it's a refund from the same counterparty the customer paid earlier, that original payment was already reviewed and closed, and the refund's amount and reference match the counterparty's confirmation. Check the refund doesn't exceed the original payment. Send an RFI if the refund comes from a different payer than the original payee, or the amount is higher than what was paid. Escalate if "refunds" from higher-risk countries repeat, come from unrelated parties, or are quickly sent on to third parties.

note: The £17,004.62 came from the customer's own account at Brightwater Bank (32-72-43 51657524), reference "OWN ACCOUNT", and the Brightwater statement in the customer's name shows the same amount sent on 10 August. So the money is the customer's own. But it takes 30-day receipts to 6.5 times declared income, and the bank's policy says own-account transfers at 5 times or more need an RFI for an updated expected income. (Labelled CLOSE OWN_ACCOUNT by Jad; changed to RFI_UPDATED_PROFILE under the 5x policy rule.)
lesson: A large credit is explained when it comes from the customer's own account at another bank and a statement in the customer's name from that bank shows the same amount and date going out. Check that the sending account number on the incoming payment matches the statement. Then apply the policy's 5x rule: if own-account transfers take activity to 5 times declared income or more, send an RFI for an updated profile; below 5 times, close. Send an RFI for source of funds if there's no statement or the account holder's name differs. Escalate if the money is quickly sent on to third parties, or own-account transfers follow recent changes to contact details or devices.

note: Student (£650/mo) paid in £21,750 cash at two branches (BK-T253053882, BK-T256188381), sent £20,900 to Parker Garmore in Spain next day (BK-T775949636); conflicting stories, gift from uncle (CHT-4600) vs car sale (CHT-681)

Classic money mule: 9 unrelated payers in 5 days forwarded to Coinvale Exchange Ltd plus ATM cash; customer admits keeping 8% for an online 'payments assistant' job (CHT-8630); two APP scam reports on incoming payments (RPT-1949, RPT-2202). Earlier review BK-R285016 covers only a holiday booking

Address-only match: BK-L62003 is Parker Kelwick at Unit 4B; REG-2766 shows Hollbrook Print Studio Ltd at Unit 4A, sole officer and PSC Toby Hartworth. RCT-4594 matches the £240 course payment of 17 Oct (BK-T807892198)

Student (£650/mo) paid in £19,850 cash at two branches (BK-T101320014, BK-T319283108), sent £19,200 to Charlie Lockby in Spain same day (BK-T976506754); conflicting stories, uncle's gift (CHT-458) vs car sale (CHT-1701)

Hospital invoice INV-9860 (18 Aug, £7,320.17, Whithurst University Medical Center, Beirut, patient Alex Halmere) matches payment BK-T877358220 of 20 Aug exactly; customer's explanation CHT-8382 consistent

Dormant 293 days; reactivated by £7,489.52 SWIFT from 'Riley Marholt' UAE account ending 4297 (BK-T284788084). No document shows customer holds that account, so own-account close not allowed; ask for statement of the UAE account / source of savings

Festival operator; cash reconciliation REC-4391 matches all four deposits by amount, point (north/south gate, main bar, food court) and banking date 8-9 Oct; ticket report TKT-8213 confirms Norworth Food Festival 6-7 Oct

Inheritance: Marwick Solicitors LLP letter SOL-9135 (10 Sep) confirms £60,356.61 share of estate of Alex Gargate; received 14 Sep from Marwick client account, ref ESTATE OF ALEX GARGATE (BK-T907864534); rest is salary
